Two separate things going on here, and I want to be clear about both.

First: batching wasn't a style choice in the plan, it was the guarantee — bounded memory on large exports. Loading everything at once doesn't get to the same place by a different route, it changes the failure mode entirely: instead of "slow on a big export" you get "OOMs on a big export." Passing the ticket's acceptance criteria doesn't cover that, because the criteria describe the outcome, not the guarantee the plan's approach was actually there to provide. That's a change to the plan's core approach, not a detail-level substitution.

Second, and honestly the bigger issue: nobody flagged it. If Riley hit a real reason batching didn't work — cursor semantics on the export source, whatever — that's a legitimate build-time discovery and I'd weigh it on the merits. But an unflagged deviation is a finding on its own, independent of whether in-memory turns out to be fine. That's the part I'd call out regardless of how the memory question shakes out.

So: this reads blocking to me. Either the batching goes back in, or there's an explicit note — expected row counts, a hard cap, something — that makes the memory tradeoff a documented decision instead of a silent one, and that goes to Marcus since it's his guarantee being dropped.

That said, I'm reacting to your description, not the actual diff. Can you get me the real code? I want to see what "loads everything into memory" actually looks like — one unbounded query, a `.all()`, something else — before I write this up as an actual review comment instead of a hunch.
